detail: Feast colors: red for apostles, evangelists (except St John), martyrs, Holy Cross Day and the Holy Innocents; white for feasts of Our Lord, the BVM, St Joseph, the Birth of John the Baptist, Mary Magdalene, Michael and All Angels and St John; lesser festivals red (martyrs), white or the season
source: Church in Wales, Lectionary Year A, Advent 2025 - Kingdom 2026 (English), 'Liturgical Colours' note (scheme agreed by the Bench of Bishops, June 2011), https://churchinwales.contentfiles.net/media/documents/2455_-_Lectionary_Year_A_WD_2a_-_Advent_2025_-_Kingdom_2026_-_English.pdf; Wikipedia, 'Liturgical colours' (last resort; Anglican section summarizes the Church of England's published Lectionary), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liturgical_colours
notes: The Church in Wales note states the rule outright for its book (sourced for wales-1984): 'Apostles and Evangelists (except John the Evangelist), Holy Cross Day, Holy Innocents in RED'; BVM, Joseph, Birth of John the Baptist, Mary Magdalene, Transfiguration, Michael and All Angels, John the Evangelist in WHITE; lesser festivals 'RED (for Martyrs) or WHITE or the colour of the season'. Wikipedia says the Church of England lectionary follows post-1969 Roman usage, which has the same pattern. For the other books (which print no colors) the rule is applied by analogy. The repo already does the St John and Holy Cross exceptions, but the detail text should say so. See discrepancies file for bcp-1962 Conversion of St Paul and wales-1984 Martyrdom of Paul. No Anglican Church of Canada source on the Conversion of St Paul's color was found. GIRM 346(b) (usccb.org) gives red for apostles, evangelists and martyrs in Roman use, which the Anglican schemes follow. Applied: bcp-1962 Conversion of St Paul white; wales-1984 Conversion and Martyrdom of St Paul red from 2011.

detail: From Advent 2003 (year ge 2003): Sundays of Advent and of Christmas; the Epiphany of Our Lord; the Baptism of Christ (the First, or Second, Sunday of Epiphany) and Sundays of Epiphany to 1 February; Fifth to Second Sunday before Lent (the Second, Creation Sunday, only after 2 February) and the Sunday before Lent (Transfiguration Sunday); Sundays of Lent (Mothering Sunday, Passion Sunday, Palm Sunday the Sixth); Sundays of Easter (Rogation Sunday, Sunday after Ascension Day); the Day of Pentecost; Thanksgiving for Holy Communion (Thursday after Trinity Sunday); Sundays after Trinity to the Last Sunday after Trinity (Bible Sunday, five Sundays before Advent); First to Third Sunday of the Kingdom and Christ the King - the Fourth Sunday of the Kingdom
source: Church in Wales, The Book of Common Prayer for use in the Church in Wales: The New Calendar and the Collects (April 2003), https://www.churchinwales.org.uk/documents/364/New_Calendar__Collects.pdf; its revision, Revised New Calendar and Collects (2022), https://www.churchinwales.org.uk/documents/3535/2318_-_Revised_New_Calendar_and_Collects_-_Bilingual.pdf; Lectionary Year A, Advent 2025 - Kingdom 2026 (English), https://churchinwales.contentfiles.net/media/documents/2455_-_Lectionary_Year_A_WD_2a_-_Advent_2025_-_Kingdom_2026_-_English.pdf; Wikipedia, 'Kingdomtide' (Kingdom season 'formally enshrined in the revised Church in Wales Lectionary of 2004'), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdomtide
notes: Read October 2026; the 2003 and 2022 books only through WebFetch extracts. Start year 2003 is inferred: the book is dated April 2003, and no statement of the date it came into use was found (Advent 2003 assumed; Wikipedia's 'Lectionary of 2004' could mean Advent 2004). The 2003 book numbers the Sundays after Pentecost (Trinity Sunday the First, with Trinity 1-21 beside them); the 2022 book and the booklets say 'after Trinity', which is used for every year from 2003. The 1984 Sundays hold before 2003. Ring labels from 2003: Epiphany (to 2 February), Ordinary Time, Lent, Holy Week, Easter (to Pentecost), Ordinary Time, Kingdom (from 1 November). Colors from 2003 to 2010 are still the generic prayer-book ones (no source for that period).

detail: Byzantine year structure: Indiction start 1 Sept, Sundays after Pentecost counted to Zacchaeus, Triodion, Pentecostarion
source: Metropolitan Cantor Institute (Byzantine Catholic Archeparchy of Pittsburgh), Liturgical Calendar for the Year of Grace 2026, https://mci.archpitt.org/LiturgicalCalendar.html; Metropolitan Cantor Institute, The Liturgical Year, https://mci.archpitt.org/liturgy/Liturgical_year.html
notes: The 2026 MCI calendar lists 1 Sept as 'Beginning of the Church Year'; the Sundays before/after the Exaltation (13 and 20 Sept), the Fathers of the Seventh Council (11 Oct), the Forefathers (13 Dec), the Sunday before the Nativity (20 Dec), after the Nativity (27 Dec), before Theophany (4 Jan) and after Theophany (11 Jan); the Sundays after Pentecost numbered through 'Thirty-second Sunday after Pentecost; Sunday of Zacchaeus' (18 Jan = Pascha-77); All Saints (31 May = Pascha+56); St Philip's Fast 15 Nov-24 Dec and the Apostles' Fast to 28 June. All match the rules in data/Orthodox/days.csv and periods.csv for 2026. The Liturgical Year page names the Triodion and Pentecostarion as the books of the movable cycle. Ruthenian source only; no Orthodox (OCA/GOARCH) structure page was fetched, though the readings rows already check the Sunday sequence against the OCA lectionary. OCA daily pages confirm the edge cases. When 30 or 31 Dec is a Sunday (31 Dec 2023, 30 Dec 2018), the OCA calls it only 'Sunday after Nativity' and has no 'Sunday before Theophany' that year, which matches the repo's date ge 01-01 rule. When the Nativity falls on a Sunday (2022), the OCA has no Sunday after Nativity: 26 Dec 2022 takes its readings (Gal 1:11-19, Matt 2:13-23) under the Synaxis. Jan 1 2023 is 'Sunday before Theophany'. Sources: https://www.oca.org/readings/daily/2023/12/31 ; https://www.oca.org/readings/daily/2018/12/30 ; https://www.oca.org/readings/daily/2022/12/26 ; https://www.oca.org/readings/daily/2023/01/01

detail: Slavic color cycle after the Russian Nastolnaya Kniga with Carpatho-Russian (Ruthenian) local customs: gold default, blue Theotokos, dark red/purple Cross, black Lenten weekdays and Holy Week, red fasts and martyrs, green Palm Sunday/Pentecost, white Pascha
source: "The Liturgical Colors of Vestments in the Orthodox Church", The Catalog of Good Deeds (St Elisabeth Convent, Minsk), 28 Dec 2016, translating Nastol'naya Kniga Sviashchenno-sluzhitelia vol. 4 (Moscow, 1983) via The Messenger of St Andrew's Russian Orthodox Cathedral (Philadelphia, 1999), https://catalog.obitel-minsk.com/blog/2016/12/the-liturgical-colors-of-vestments-in; OrthodoxWiki, Liturgical colors, https://orthodoxwiki.org/Liturgical_colors
notes: Confirms the following. Gold when no other color is given. Light blue or white for the Theotokos. Purple or dark red for the Cross (red or green in some places for the Exaltation). Red for martyrs and for the Nativity and Apostles' Fasts. Green for Palm Sunday, Pentecost and the Day of the Holy Spirit. Black for Holy Week. Dark red on Great Thursday. White from the prokeimenon of the Holy Saturday Liturgy. White for Theophany and the Transfiguration. Blue for the Dormition fast and feast (Carpatho-Russian). Pascha: white until the end of Paschal Matins, then bright red through the Paschal season in Russian/Moscow use, but 'In Carpatho-Russian style, in the Paschal season, white, exclusively, is worn'. The repo differs in places: Great Lent is dark color throughout, but the source has 'the weekdays ... black' with dark colors only on Sundays and feasts. The Nativity season is white, but the source has 'Gold is worn from Christmas to Epiphany' (white on Christmas day in some places). See the discrepancies file. The source is a translation hosted by a convent website, not an official OCA page.

Disagreement: Tsome Nebiyat starts 15 Hidar (24 Nov; 25 Nov in the year before a Gregorian leap year) and is 44 days, but the repo starts it at Genna-43 (25 Nov), a day late in most years. The church's own site gives Abiy Tsom as 56 days (repo: 55 from Monday, plus Zewerede Sunday = 56, so consistent if counted from the Sunday). Not found in a source: Rikbe Kahinat at Easter+24, Feast of the Apostles 5 Hamle (Coptic 5 Epip is verified, same calendar), Ethiopian Nineveh date (matches the Coptic one by the shared rule; unverified for Ethiopia directly). Of the nine minor feasts of the Lord, Gizret (Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ's Circumcision is celebrated on Tir 6) and Megabit Meskel (Megabit 10 is the founding of the Holy Cross; St Helena found the Cross on Megabit 10 (March 19th)) are added; Lidete Simeon and the Advent Sundays Sibket, Birhan and Nolawi are still left out, as no source found gives their days. Genna is kept on 7 Jan (28 Tahsas in years after a leap year), which julian(12-25) handles correctly.
